findings.where: Phone hero: the order of the headline, the yellow address strip and the 'I advise multilateral development banks…' line
findings.fault: On the phone, the yellow strip with the address comes straight after the headline, and the line saying what Mark does and for whom comes after the strip, below the first phone screen. On desktop, that line comes before the address. On the phone, the strip also stops being 'at the foot of the sheet', where the tile's own texture note puts it. A phone visitor is asked to write before being told what he advises on and for whom. The only clue above the fold is the 'Formerly Lead Lawyer' credential.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer opening the site on a phone from a LinkedIn link would object, because they need to know what he does for bodies like theirs before writing (first-visit trust item 2). The founder would also object, because the phone sheet breaks the letter idea the tile sets out (the address at the foot of the sheet).

findings.where: Article specimen: the lectern photograph, desktop and phone
findings.fault: The article photo is turned to greyscale, and its backdrop is darkened to a near-black slab about 640 px wide. It is the heaviest thing in the article, heavier than the article heading. The flat grey newspaper treatment loses the 'real people in real light' and the grading into the house colours that the research asks for. On a calm ivory page, a large greyscale portrait of a living man can read as a press or obituary photo, not as an advisor at work.
findings.who_objects: The founder would object, because the brief's research asks for real people in real light, with imagery graded into the house blue-grey (a.3, F4), not desaturated. Mark would object too, because the treatment makes him look like a man in the news rather than a warm, personal advisor.

findings.where: Article specimen: the Download link 'Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the ‘Abundance’ Challenge'
findings.fault: The link is labelled and dated as a PDF lecture, but the parts map shows it goes to '#'. Clicking it does nothing, even though the PDFs are the product the research says the page exists to show.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who clicks it expecting the lecture and gets nothing would object. So would the founder, who is judging whether the PDF list works as the product (research a.6).

findings.where: Article specimen, desktop: the Download row's details 'Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF'
findings.fault: The format and date sit right-aligned at the far edge of the column, about 100 px past the end of the link's first line. They read as a separate item, not as the label of the link beside them. On the phone, they sit directly under the link.
findings.who_objects: A reader scanning for 'is this a PDF, and how recent is it' would object, because they have to jump across empty space to tie the details to the link. With several rows in a real list, the details could be matched to the wrong one.

findings.where: Motion section, the 'Replay the entrance' control (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The parts map shows it is a button, but it is drawn in the link's blue with an underline, like the nav and article links. An action borrows the look the page reserves for links that go somewhere.
findings.who_objects: A keyboard or screen-reader user, or a careful reviewer, would object, because they expect an underlined blue phrase to take them somewhere, not to replay something in place. It also blurs the rule that blue underline means a link.

findings.where: Motion section: the easing-curve box, desktop and phone
findings.fault: The curve's box is inset about 7 px from the column's left edge, while its caption, the 'Settled, unhurried, once.' heading and every other block above line up on that edge. It looks like a slip, not a choice.
findings.who_objects: The founder, judging craft, would object, because a visible misalignment undercuts the 'refined' claim of a tile built on one hairline and a strict column.

findings.where: Type pair specimen: 'Profile · Articles · Blog' in Public Sans
findings.fault: The sans is shown at about 34 px medium weight, though the note beside it says the page only ever uses it at 13–15 px. At that size it looks heavier and louder than it ever will on the site, which misstates how the pair feels.
findings.who_objects: The founder, deciding on the type pair from this specimen, would object, because they would be judging a sans that never appears at that size.

findings.where: First screen: the headline and the supporting line beneath it
findings.fault: The headline writes 'public-private partnerships' in lower case, and the draft line just below writes 'Public-Private Partnerships' with capitals. The same term appears in two forms, one above the other, on the first screen.
findings.who_objects: A lawyer or development-bank reader, who notices inconsistent defined terms, would object. So would Mark, whose draft line is meant to sit with his own words.
